input: Label and archive all work project files by client

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing which files and file types are included (e.g. all formats vs. specific ones, active vs. completed projects) determines the size and boundaries of the task.
Whether this is a solo effort or involves teammates affects coordination, permissions, and whether a shared naming convention needs to be agreed upon first.
Where the files currently live (local drive, cloud storage like Google Drive/Dropbox, a project management tool) dictates which tools and methods are available for labelling and archiving.
A deadline or time budget changes whether this is a quick sweep or a thorough multi-session project, and whether automation is worth setting up.
The preferred folder/label structure (e.g. by client name, then year, then project type) directly shapes the naming convention and archive hierarchy to build.
Knowing what 'done well' looks like — findability, a clean root folder, a consistent naming scheme — sets the quality bar and prevents re-doing work.
Whether files should be deleted, compressed, or simply moved, and whether originals need to stay accessible, affects the exact archiving steps to take.

gold.taskTitle: Label and archive work project files by client
gold.taskDescription: Organise all existing work project files by applying clear labels and moving them into a structured archive sorted by client.

questions.title: Which file types and project statuses are included?
questions.description: Clarify whether all file formats are in scope or only specific ones (e.g. PDFs, design files, spreadsheets), and whether both active and completed projects should be archived or only finished ones.

questions.title: Will anyone else be accessing or managing these files?
questions.description: Determine if this is a solo task or if colleagues, assistants, or clients also need access, which would require agreed-upon conventions and shared permissions.

questions.title: Where do the files currently live?
questions.description: Identify the storage location — local hard drive, a cloud service like Google Drive or Dropbox, a network drive, or a project management platform — as this dictates the available tools.

questions.title: Is there a deadline by which this needs to be done?
questions.description: Establish whether there is a hard due date or a time limit per session, which determines how much to prioritise speed versus thoroughness and whether automation is worth the setup time.

questions.title: What folder hierarchy do you want inside each client folder?
questions.description: Define the preferred sub-structure under each client, such as organising by year, project name, file type, or a combination, to build a consistent and reusable template.

questions.title: How will you know the archive is good enough to stop?
questions.description: Identify the success markers — for example, every file is findable in under 30 seconds, the root folder is empty, or every file follows the naming convention — to define a clear finishing point.

questions.title: Should originals be deleted, compressed, or kept after archiving?
questions.description: Decide what happens to files after they are moved — whether originals are deleted, zipped to save space, or left in place — and whether archived files still need to be readily openable.
